explanations.answer: The Nile is mine and I made it myself
explanations.explanation: That's the brag, word for word: "The Nile is mine; I made it myself." (Ezekiel 29:3) Pharaoh, Egypt's king, takes all the credit. That's like a guy walking into my bakery and announcing he invented the oven. Friend, sit DOWN.

explanations.answer: The Nile was handed to me by my gods
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not what Pharaoh says. He doesn't give anybody else a thank-you. He says, "The Nile is mine; I made it myself." (Ezekiel 29:3) The only name in that sentence is his own.

explanations.answer: The Nile will flow forever just for me
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like something a king might say, but it's not in the text. Pharaoh's claim is about who made the river: "The Nile is mine; I made it myself." (Ezekiel 29:3) He's not promising the river anything. He's pointing at himself.

God says it plainly: "I will haul you up out of your rivers, and all the fish of your streams will cling to your scales." (Ezekiel 29:4) So the fish come along for the ride. Nobody on that riverbank asked for passengers. I think those fish had a rough morning.
You'd think mud, right? A river's full of it. But the text never mentions mud. What clings to his scales is "the fish of your streams." (Ezekiel 29:4)
Frogs are a fun guess, but they aren't in this verse. God says, "all the fish of your streams will cling to your scales." (Ezekiel 29:4) It's fish, baker. Fish all the way down.
This one's tricky, so no shame. The text goes the other way. God says, "You will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial." (Ezekiel 29:5) No proper burial is coming.

Right, it's False. God says, "You will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial." (Ezekiel 29:5) Nobody comes to pick him up. That's a heavy line, so I'll just let it sit.

That's the whole point. God says, "Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 29:6) Pharaoh said the Nile was his own work. By the end, everybody in Egypt knows who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: That their gods have left them
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, but this verse doesn't say a word about their gods. What it says is that all the people of Egypt "will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 29:6) God keeps the focus on Himself.

explanations.answer: That their king has run away
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody runs anywhere in this verse. Pharaoh is given "as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air," and then the people of Egypt "will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 29:5-6) That's what they come to know.
Reeds it is: "you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 29:6) A reed looks like a walking stick until you put your weight on it. Then it's a bad day for your shoulders.
Cedar's a fine, strong wood, so I see the guess. But God says Egypt was "only a staff of reeds." (Ezekiel 29:6) Reeds are thin, and they don't hold up when somebody leans.
If it were iron, Israel could lean all day and nothing would happen. That's the opposite of what God says. Egypt was "only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 29:6)

explanations.answer: It splinters and tears their shoulders
explanations.explanation: God says, "When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders." (Ezekiel 29:7) They grabbed it for help and it hurt them instead. That's a rough trade, friend.

explanations.answer: It holds but bends down low
explanations.explanation: A staff that holds would be good news for Israel. That's not what happens. The text says "you splintered, tearing all their shoulders." (Ezekiel 29:7)

explanations.answer: It sinks into the soft mud
explanations.explanation: No mud in this verse. The staff doesn't sink, it breaks. When Israel took hold, it "splintered, tearing all their shoulders." (Ezekiel 29:7)
That's right. God says, "I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast." (Ezekiel 29:8) This is a hard word. It's the Lord GOD speaking about Egypt, and He says it plainly.

It's actually True. Here are God's words: "Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast." (Ezekiel 29:8) It's a heavy verse, and it's really there.

Rivers is right. After the Nile brag, God says, "therefore I am against you and against your rivers." (Ezekiel 29:10) Pharaoh claimed the river as his own work. So the rivers get named right alongside him.
Chariots sound like a king's kind of target, but the verse never mentions them. God says, "I am against you and against your rivers." (Ezekiel 29:10) It lines up with the Nile brag.
Priests aren't in this verse at all. The words are "therefore I am against you and against your rivers." (Ezekiel 29:10) It goes back to what Pharaoh said about the Nile.

explanations.answer: No man or beast will pass through
explanations.explanation: That's it: "No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years." (Ezekiel 29:11) Not one foot, baker. It's about as quiet as a bakery after the last cookie is gone.
That would leave a little traffic, but God doesn't say so. The text says, "No foot of man or beast will pass through." (Ezekiel 29:11) That means no exceptions listed.
Traders don't get a pass here. God says, "No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years." (Ezekiel 29:11) The road is empty.

The first half is right, but the second half is where it trips. God says, "I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries." (Ezekiel 29:12) So they're not staying home together. They're scattered while the land sits empty.

Right, it's False. The land is uninhabited for forty years, and God says, "I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries." (Ezekiel 29:12) They're spread out, not together at home.

explanations.answer: Gather them back from the nations
explanations.explanation: God says, "At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered." (Ezekiel 29:13) After all that scattering, there's a gathering. I like how the story doesn't stop at the hard part.

That's what verse 12 might leave you thinking, but God keeps talking. He says, "At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered." (Ezekiel 29:13) Forty years is the number He gives.

This verse says nothing about servants. What God says is, "At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered." (Ezekiel 29:13) That's the plan on the table.

Lowly is it: "There they will be a lowly kingdom." (Ezekiel 29:14) They're back in Pathros, the land of their origin, but not on top. God goes further in the next verse, calling Egypt "the lowliest of kingdoms." (Ezekiel 29:15)
Mighty is the opposite of what God says. Egypt returns, but as "a lowly kingdom." (Ezekiel 29:14) The very next verse calls it "the lowliest of kingdoms." (Ezekiel 29:15)
Divided isn't a word God uses here. He says, "There they will be a lowly kingdom." (Ezekiel 29:14) The word to hold onto is lowly.

I can see why a comeback story sounds nice, but God says no. "Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations." (Ezekiel 29:15) That one stays False, friend.

Right, False. God says Egypt "will never again exalt itself above the nations," and adds, "I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations." (Ezekiel 29:15) It gets to come home, but not to the top.

explanations.answer: Their sin in turning to Egypt
explanations.explanation: God says Egypt "will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians." (Ezekiel 29:16) Iniquity is sin. So Egypt stops being a place to lean and becomes a reminder of leaning in the wrong place.

explanations.answer: Their years as slaves in Egypt
explanations.explanation: It's a good Egypt memory, but it's not what this verse says. God says Egypt "will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians." (Ezekiel 29:16) The reminder is about turning to Egypt.

explanations.answer: Their escape across the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: The Red Sea doesn't come up in this passage. God says Egypt will be "a reminder of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians." (Ezekiel 29:16) That's the memory He names.

You'd expect a paycheck after all that work, but the text says otherwise. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his army "received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it." (Ezekiel 29:18) Tyre is the city they worked against. All that work, and the pay never came.

Right, False. The text says Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his army "received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it." (Ezekiel 29:18) That's a lot of hard work with nothing in the envelope.
Egypt is right. God says, "I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon." (Ezekiel 29:19) Remember, Pharaoh was king of Egypt. That's where this land change is headed.
Wages is the word. God says, "This will be the wages for his army." (Ezekiel 29:19) The army worked and didn't get paid by Tyre. Here God names where the pay comes from.

Tyre is the city the army worked against, and it paid them nothing. The land going to Nebuchadnezzar is Egypt. God says, "I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon." (Ezekiel 29:19)
Edom doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. The land God gives is Egypt. He says, "I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon." (Ezekiel 29:19)
Ransom is a different kind of payment, and God doesn't use the word here. He says, "This will be the wages for his army." (Ezekiel 29:19) The word you want is wages.

explanations.answer: Because the labor was done for God
explanations.explanation: God says, "I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me." (Ezekiel 29:20) That's the reason, and it's stated right there. The labor was for Him.

explanations.answer: Because Babylon begged God for it
explanations.explanation: There's no begging anywhere in this verse. God gives His reason: "I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me." (Ezekiel 29:20) The reason is the labor.
The text never says that. It gives a different reason: "I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me." (Ezekiel 29:20) It all comes back to the labor.
That's right. God says, "I will open your mouth to speak among them." (Ezekiel 29:21) He's talking to Ezekiel here. I think that's a nice way to end a heavy chapter.

This one's actually True. God says, "In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them." (Ezekiel 29:21) He's speaking to Ezekiel, and the promise is right there.
